newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel claims victory at White House summit.
newsitem.headline: Israel claims victory at White House summit.

text.p: Israel claimed victory at an emergency White House summit aimed at quelling the explosion of violence in the Middle East, but Palestinians called it a failure which could plunge the region further into turmoil.
"The results of the summit are a great success from the point of view of the government of Israel," Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel radio from Washington after the Wednesday talks.
"The peace process is on the verge of collapse," said Mustafa Natsheh, Palestinian mayor of Hebron on the West Bank.
"Unless international and Arab public opinion and Israeli peace groups move, the area will not witness any calm and the cycle of violence will return anew," he said.

President Bill Clinton told a White House news conference after the two-day summit that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israel's new right-wing prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had failed to resolve their differences. He acknowledged the Middle East peace process was still in crisis.

He said the two sides had agreed to resume immediate peace talks focusing on an Israeli pullback from Hebron. But this was far less than the immediate Israeli redeployment from the flashpoint city which Arafat had demanded.
"The summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence," Hasan Asfour, a PLO negotiator, told Reuters. "I hope that the Arab nation has realised what awaits us."

Besides a Hebron pullback, Arafat had demanded that Netanyahu close a tunnel near Moslem shrines in Arab Jerusalem which sparked violence that has killed 58 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers in recent days.
Arafat, who looked grim and said nothing at the news conference with Clinton, came away empty-handed.
Khaled Salam, a close Arafat adviser, said Clinton had done his best to salvage the summit.
"But it is clear, and this is my personal opinion, that with Mr Netanyahu it is easier to enter a war than to reach peace," he told Reuters.
"This is a man whose policies are providing every possibility for a war. I hope I am wrong."
Right-wing Israelis and Jewish settlers in Palestinian areas welcomed Netanyahu's tough stance.
"I am very glad about the prime minister's firm stance. On the other hand I'm worried about the Palestinian reaction," said Pinchas Wallerstein, head of the settlers' umbrella council.

Israel has ringed Palestinian-ruled towns with tanks and put the army on alert since unprecedented gunbattles with Arafat's lightly-armed police, who said they opened fire after Israeli soldiers shot stone-throwing protesters.
Israeli security officials fear that Palestinian anger at the slow pace of self-rule could again erupt in violence because of the lack of concrete gains from Washington.
"The look (on Arafat's face) is very gloomy," said Palestinian legislator Dalal Salameh from Nablus.
"The situation is miserable and does not call for optimism. There is deep disappointment as far as the tunnel is concerned," he said.
